Triggers.value: The same time of day the event occurred

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

vignette: As she unlocked the door to her small shop, Leilani's mind began to wander back to that fateful evening, three years ago. It was around 8 pm when the police stormed in, responding to a false tip about a robbery in progress. The memory of the sound of shattering glass and the feeling of being thrown to the ground still made her skin crawl. She couldn't shake off the sense of being watched, even now, as she went about her daily routine. The same time of day always brought back the anxiety; Leilani found herself glancing over her shoulder, expecting to see someone lurking in the shadows. Her eyes would scan the empty streets, and for a moment, she'd feel like she was back in that terrifying moment. The dizziness that accompanied these episodes made it hard for her to focus on anything else. Leilani had developed a habit of avoiding circumstances that reminded her of the event. She refused to be alone in the shop after dark, always making sure to close up by 6 pm sharp. She'd also stopped attending community events and gatherings, fearing she might see one of the officers involved in the incident. The anniversaries were especially tough; Leilani would go into a funk for days, unable to muster the energy to do anything but stay in bed. Compulsive spending had become another way for her to cope with the anxiety. She'd buy things she didn't need - clothes, kitchen gadgets, anything that caught her eye - just to distract herself from the thoughts swirling in her head. Her shop's inventory had grown exponentially, and while it might look like a successful business to outsiders, Leilani knew it was just a facade. The memory of that night still felt unreal to Leilani. There were parts she couldn't remember no matter how hard she tried - fragments of conversation, the faces of the officers, the sound of her own screams. She'd try to put the pieces together, but it was like trying to assemble a puzzle with missing parts. When people asked her about that night, Leilani found herself struggling to put the words together; it was as if her mind had created a nonverbal shorthand for the trauma. The shame and inadequacy she felt still lingered. Why hadn't she fought back? Why had she let them push her around like that? The questions swirled in her head, making her feel like she was indeed a "lousy coper." Leilani worried that her reactions since the event meant she was losing her grip on reality - that she was going crazy. She'd catch herself staring at nothing, lost in thought, and wonder if this was what it felt like to unravel. As the days turned into weeks, and the weeks into months, Leilani's relationships with her friends and family began to fray. They didn't understand why she couldn't just "get over" the incident, why she couldn't just move on. The isolation had become overwhelming; Leilani felt like she was drowning in a sea of uncertainty. It was only when her accountant sat her down and explained that her shop was on the verge of bankruptcy - thanks to her compulsive spending - that Leilani realized she needed help. She couldn't keep living like this, trapped in a cycle of fear and avoidance. As she looked around her cluttered shop, Leilani knew it was time to face the memories head-on, no matter how painful they might be.
